newsitem.title: USA: Oil soars to post-Gulf War high on Iraq action.
newsitem.headline: Oil soars to post-Gulf War high on Iraq action.

text.p: Oil prices soared to post Gulf War highs Tuesday as the U.S. market returned from a holiday weekend to news of U.S. military strikes in Iraq and the U.N. decision to call off plans for the resumption of Iraqi oil exports.

In lively trading, October crude oil jumped $1.70 to $23.95 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange. Oil prices are now at their highest levels since October 1990, when Iraq invaded Kuwait. The U.S. market was closed Monday for the Labour Day holiday.
Although prices are still below the record high of $40.95 a barrel hit during the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait in 1990, they are $6 higher than at this time last year.
October unleaded gasoline gained 3.49 cents to 65.10 a gallon and heating oil was up 3.28 cents to 66.40 a gallon.

The London oil market was up 63 cents at $22.60 a barrel Tuesday after soaring $1.29 per barrel Monday as Iraqi military activity in the Kurdish north prompted the United Nations to freeze plans to allow Iraq to sell $2 billion in oil to pay for food and medical supplies.
The United States on Tuesday responded to the Iraqi Kurdish attack by firing missiles at Iraqi military targets in the south of the country.
Iraqi military intervention in Kurd fighting took place at a time when global oil reserves are low and demand is booming.
Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's latest military move was expected to derail plans for the resumption of Iraqi oil exports beyond the end of the year.
"Most people were looking for a correction in the oil price once Iraq supplies returned -- that's now been postponed into 1997 and possibly as late as the spring," said one analyst.
Traders had been expecting Baghdad in the next few weeks to make its first oil sale on world markets since Gulf War sanctions were imposed six years ago.
"Iraqi oil is not on the agenda until after the U.S. election," said Charles Gray, an analyst at Prudential Bache in London.
Added Mari Buglass, senior energy analyst at Smith Barney, "We probably will not see Iraqi oil this year. The U.N. will argue that it is still not safe to send their workers in."
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said Baghdad would complete a withdrawal of troops from Kurdistan later on Tuesday.
But Saddam, in a televised address urged Iraqi troops to resist the U.S. attack and said he would no longer recognise "no fly zones" policed by allied warplanes over northern and southern Iraq.
The Iraqi leader has done more to bolster oil prices in recent years than all his fellow members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries put together.
"Poor Saddam is helping to improve the income of his Gulf War enemies Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. OPEC should be very pleased with his work," a senior OPEC official said.
Ever since Saddam stunned the world with his invasion of Kuwait in 1990, oil prices have gyrated on his every move.
OPEC recently seemed ready to collapse when faced with having to set new production quotas to take account of the easing of the U.N.'s Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil sales.
"You could say that Saddam is oil's hidden benefactor. With prices being where they are now, OPEC members themselves see no reason to cut production," said Smith, Barney's Buglass.
